props.title: Click
props.initialSlug: Life's greatest moments can't be rewound.

sections.content: Click (2006) represents Adam Sandler's most effective blend of comedy and drama, following the pattern of Jim Carrey's Bruce Almighty (2003) in using supernatural elements to explore life's deeper meanings. The universal remote control premise taps into our fantasy of controlling time, similar to Back to the Future (1985), but delivers a gut-punch message about taking life's small moments for granted. Director Frank Coraci balances Sandler's trademark humor with surprisingly heavy themes about workaholism and family neglect that resonated with mid-2000s audiences dealing with work-life balance struggles.

sections.content: The film's emotional core draws surprising parallels with It's a Wonderful Life (1946), as both protagonists get supernatural glimpses of how their choices affect loved ones. Like 13 Going on 30 (2004), Click uses its magical premise to examine the consequences of wishing away "boring" parts of life. The scenes where Michael Newman fast-forwards through family dinners and bedtime stories hit particularly hard because they reflect real behaviors in our smartphone-obsessed culture.

The visual effects, while dated by today's standards, effectively convey time's passage through subtle aging makeup and environmental changes. This technical approach echoes The Curious Case of Benjamin Button (2008), though used for opposite effect. Christopher Walken's mysterious Morty character follows a rich tradition of supernatural guides like Clarence from It's a Wonderful Life (1946) and Don Ameche in Trading Places (1983). sections.content: While marketed as a typical Sandler comedy, Click's third act transforms into a powerful meditation on mortality and regret. This dramatic shift mirrors similar genre-blending efforts like Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind (2004) and The Truman Show (1998). The film's message about being present in life's moments has only grown more relevant in our era of constant digital distraction, making it a prescient warning about technology's ability to disconnect us from real human connection.
